newsitem.title: USA: CBOT SOYBEANS END MOSTLY HIGHER ON WEATHER JITTERS.
newsitem.headline: CBOT SOYBEANS END MOSTLY HIGHER ON WEATHER JITTERS.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures ended mostly higher on Friday with new crop months leading the way amid uncertain weekend weather prospects, traders said.

"At midsession, people got the weather hives," said Bill Biedermann, director of research for Allendale Inc. "One of the forecasters reduced the precip forecast for Illinois and (prices) went nuts. We all got really scared and broke out in rashes and said it doesn't look like it's going to rain."
Weather Services Corp said in its afternoon update that a storm would hit the U.S. Midwest on Saturday and Sunday, bringing 0.25 to 0.75 inch with 40 to 50 percent coverage.

WSC said that storm would favor the Ohio Valley. A second storm should hit on Monday with scattered to widely scattered showers and thunderstorms of 0.25 to 0.75 inch with 40 to 50 percent coverage. That system would favor Missouri and the Ohio Valley, WSC said.

Pit sources said trade would likely be volatile on Sunday night and Monday as the market assessed weekend rainfall amounts and coverage. Moisture was considered crucial for soybeans as they set and fill pods.
Soybeans ended 12-1/2 cents per bushel higher to 5-3/4 cents lower with November up nine at $6.37-1/2.
USDA on Monday said 38 percent of the crop was setting pods. Dry weather during this stage can cut yield potential and some areas of the U.S. Midwest have received subpar rainfall this summer.
WSC said rainfall in Peoria over the last 30 days totalled 0.92 inch, or roughly 25 percent of normal. In Indianapolis, the 30-day rainfall was 14 percent of normal.
This weekend was viewed as critical for soybeans as more of the crop enters the pod setting phase.
The Conrad Leslie-ADM Elevator survey Friday estimated U.S. soy production at 2.713 billion bushels, above an average of analysts' estimate for 2.680 billion.
But traders said the market had already seen similarly large production estimates and priced in a record crop.
Volume was said to be thin ahead of Tuesday's USDA crop production report. Analysts expected the report to show a record crop in the fields.

On the day, Refco Inc bought 2.5 million bushels November and sold 1.5 million November and two million August. Griffin Trading sold two million November and Dean Witter sold one million November, traders said.

In spread action, E.D. and F. Man International spread 1.5 million August/November at $1.15 to $1.20, premium August. Farmers Commodities Corp, Smith Barney and LFG were also said to be bull spreaders.
In options, Lind-Waldock bought 550 January $6.75 calls at 21 to 22-1/2, Produce Grain sold 200 November $6.75 calls at 16 cents and bought 200 November $6.00 puts at 16.
Volatility in the November was pegged at 27 percent, against Thursday's 27-1/2 percent.
Soybean futures volume was estimated by CBOT at 40,000 contracts, compared with Thursday's actual volume of 47,384.
